problems.title: Binary Search
problems.statement: Given an array of integers nums sorted in ascending order and a target integer target, write a function to search target in nums. Return index if present else -1.
problems.understanding: Eliminate half of the remaining search space on each step in a sorted array.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Scan every element linearly from index 0 to n-1.

problems.intuition: Use two pointers left and right. Calculate mid = left + (right - left) // 2. If nums[mid] == target return mid, else adjust boundaries.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize left = 0, right = len(nums) - 1.
  2. Loop while left <= right:
  3. Compute mid = left + (right - left) // 2.
  4. If nums[mid] == target, return mid.
  5. If nums[mid] < target, set left = mid + 1.
  6. Else, set right = mid - 1.
  7. Return -1 if target not found.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Sorted array → Eliminate half → Standard Binary Search

problems.title: Search a 2D Matrix
problems.statement: Write an efficient algorithm that searches for a value target in an m x n integer matrix where each row is sorted and the first element of each row is greater than the last of the previous row.
problems.understanding: The entire matrix behaves like one contiguous sorted 1D array of size m * n.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Nested row and column loops checking every matrix cell.

problems.intuition: Treat 2D matrix as a virtual 1D sorted array of length rows * cols. Map 1D index to 2D cell via: row = index // cols, col = index % cols.
problems.approach:
1. Set left = 0, right = rows * cols - 1.
  2. Loop while left <= right:
  3. Compute mid = left + (right - left) // 2.
  4. Map row = mid // cols, col = mid % cols.
  5. If matrix[row][col] == target, return True.
  6. If matrix[row][col] < target, left = mid + 1; else right = mid - 1.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — 2D Matrix with sorted boundaries → Virtual 1D Binary Search

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.statement: Koko can decide her eating speed k per hour. Return minimum integer k such that she can eat all bananas within h hours.
problems.understanding: The answer space of speeds $k \in [1, \max(\text{piles})]$ is monotonic: if speed $k$ is valid, all speeds $> k$ are also valid.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Linear search trying every speed $k = 1, 2, 3 \dots \max(\text{piles})$ and checking total hours.

problems.intuition: Binary search on the answer space range $[1, \max(\text{piles})]$. Find the first speed where total hours $\le h$.
problems.approach:
1. Set left = 1, right = max(piles).
  2. Loop while left <= right:
  3. Set speed = left + (right - left) // 2.
  4. Compute hours = sum((pile + speed - 1) // speed for pile in piles).
  5. If hours <= h: speed is valid! Record answer = speed and try smaller speeds right = speed - 1.
  6. Else: speed is too slow, try faster speeds left = speed + 1.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Monotonic feasibility condition → Binary Search on Answer

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement: Given sorted rotated array of unique elements nums, return the minimum element in $O(\log n)$ time.
problems.understanding: The minimum element is the pivot point separating the two sorted halves.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Linear scan keeping track of minimum value.

problems.intuition: Compare nums[mid] against the right boundary nums[right]. If nums[mid] > nums[right], minimum lies in right half; else minimum lies in left half including mid.
problems.approach:
1. Set left = 0, right = len(nums) - 1.
  2. Loop while left < right:
  3. Compute mid = left + (right - left) // 2.
  4. If nums[mid] > nums[right]: minimum must be in right half left = mid + 1.
  5. Else: minimum could be mid or to the left right = mid.
  6. Return nums[left].
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Rotated sorted array → Compare mid with right boundary

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement: Given array nums rotated at an unknown pivot and integer target, return index of target or -1 in $O(\log n)$ time.
problems.understanding: At least one half of the array (left or right) is guaranteed to be strictly sorted at any step.
problems.intuition: Check if nums[left] <= nums[mid]. If True, left half is sorted: check if target is inside [nums[left], nums[mid]). Else right half is sorted: check if target is inside (nums[mid], nums[right]].
problems.approach:
1. Set left = 0, right = len(nums) - 1.
  2. Loop while left <= right:
  3. If nums[mid] == target, return mid.
  4. If nums[left] <= nums[mid] (Left half sorted):
  5. If nums[left] <= target < nums[mid], move right = mid - 1; else left = mid + 1.
  6. Else (Right half sorted):
  7. If nums[mid] < target <= nums[right], move left = mid + 1; else right = mid - 1.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Rotated array → Identify sorted half → Binary search boundary

problems.title: Time Based Key-Value Store
problems.statement: Design a key-value data structure that can store multiple values for the same key at different timestamps and retrieve key value at timestamp_prev <= timestamp.
problems.understanding: Timestamps for a key are added in strictly increasing order, so timestamps per key are sorted.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Store list of (timestamp, value) tuples and scan backward linearly on get().

problems.intuition: Binary search for the rightmost element whose timestamp $\le$ requested timestamp.
problems.approach:
1. set(key, val, time): append (time, val) to list store[key].
  2. get(key, target_time): binary search values = store[key].
  3. While left <= right:
  4. If values[mid][0] <= target_time: record answer = values[mid][1] and search right left = mid + 1.
  5. Else: search left right = mid - 1.
  6. Return answer.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Sorted timestamps → Rightmost valid binary search

problems.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.statement: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of size m and n respectively, return the median of the two sorted arrays in $O(\log(m+n))$ time.
problems.understanding: Partition both arrays into equal left and right halves such that $\max(\text{left}_1, \text{left}_2) \le \min(\text{right}_1, \text{right}_2)$.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Merge both sorted arrays into a combined array of size $m+n$ and pick median.

problems.intuition: Binary search partition on the smaller array nums1. Calculate partition indices in both arrays so total left elements equals total right elements.
problems.approach:
1. Ensure len(nums1) <= len(nums2) (swap if necessary).
  2. Set left = 0, right = len(nums1).
  3. Calculate partition1 = (left + right) // 2 and partition2 = (m + n + 1) // 2 - partition1.
  4. Determine left1, right1, left2, right2 boundary values.
  5. If left1 <= right2 and left2 <= right1: partition is valid!
  6. Return $\max(\text{left}_1, \text{left}_2)$ (if odd total length) or average of max left and min right (if even).
  7. If left1 > right2: move partition left right = partition1 - 1; else move right left = partition1 + 1.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Binary search partition on smaller array
